power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

text.text: This study identified session-level patterns of therapists' and clients' perceptions of the therapeutic alliance and treatment progress and examined whether these patterns were associated with client-reported outcomes.
Data included 15 therapist trainees, 86 clients, and 1,035 session ratings.
After each session, therapists and clients separately provided ratings, and clients rated their personal functioning and psychological symptoms.
A multilevel latent class analysis identified five session patterns: "all-high" (53.3%), "bond-focused" (16.3%), "goals/tasksfocused" (3.3%), "client-low" (18.5%), and "all-low" (8.5%).

Longitudinal multilevel models revealed lower current personal functioning after client-low sessions, than after all-high or bondfocused sessions, and higher current psychological symptoms after client-low sessions than after all-high sessions.
Clients reported higher next-session symptoms after client-low sessions than after all-high or bond-focused sessions.
No difference was detected in outcomes between all-low or goals/tasks-focused sessions and the rest.
This study has significant implications for treatment planning, monitoring of the therapeutic alliance, and supervision of therapists-in-training.

Therapeutic work involves a partnership in which therapists and clients pursue meaningful changes through communication, collaboration, and active participation (Bordin, 1979; Flückiger et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Therapeutic work involves a partnership in which therapists and clients pursue meaningful changes through communication, collaboration, and active participation <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bordin, 1979;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Flückiger et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Although participating in the same sessions, therapists and clients may perceive and experience the therapy differently (Igra et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Although participating in the same sessions, therapists and clients may perceive and experience the therapy differently <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Igra et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Their evaluations may also emphasize different aspects of treatment, including the quality of their collaboration and perceived progress.
Considering these perspectives together may offer a fuller understanding of the therapeutic process and its associations with client functioning and symptoms (Tryon et al., 2007).
text.formatted: Considering these perspectives together may offer a fuller understanding of the therapeutic process and its associations with client functioning and symptoms <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Tryon et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: The present study examined session-level configurations of client-rated therapeutic alliance and therapist-rated alliance and progress.
Client ratings captured bond, agreement on goals, and collaboration on tasks, whereas therapist ratings captured overall alliance, withinsession progress, and progress toward treatment goals.
These related but distinct evaluations characterize how clients and therapists perceive aspects of a session.
Building on prior research, we aimed to identify session-rating profiles and examined their associations with client-reported functioning and symptoms at the current and subsequent sessions.
Therapist and client perceptions of therapy overlap, but they are not interchangeable.

The most researched area within this was their perceptions of therapeutic alliance. Bordin's (1979) transtheoretical model defines the alliance through three interrelated components: agreement on the goals of treatment, agreement on the tasks needed to achieve those goals, and the affective bond between the therapist and client.
text.formatted: The most researched area within this was their perceptions of therapeutic alliance. <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Bordin's (1979)</ref> transtheoretical model defines the alliance through three interrelated components: agreement on the goals of treatment, agreement on the tasks needed to achieve those goals, and the affective bond between the therapist and client.

text.text: A large body of literature demonstrates that stronger therapeutic alliances are associated with better therapy outcomes, with an overall allianceoutcome association of approximately r = .23 to .31 across meta-analytic evidence (e.g., Flückiger et al., 2018; Flückiger, Del Re, et al., 2020).
text.formatted: A large body of literature demonstrates that stronger therapeutic alliances are associated with better therapy outcomes, with an overall allianceoutcome association of approximately r = .23 to .31 across meta-analytic evidence (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Flückiger et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Flückiger, Del Re, et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: In terms of therapist-client separate ratings on alliance measures, Tryon et al.'s (2007) meta-analysis of 53 studies found a modest client-therapist correlation of r = .36.
text.formatted: In terms of therapist-client separate ratings on alliance measures, <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Tryon et al.'s (2007)</ref> meta-analysis of 53 studies found a modest client-therapist correlation of r = .36.

text.text: Clients also gave significantly higher alliance ratings than therapists, with a standardized mean difference of d = .63.
Discrepancies were particularly pronounced in some less severely symptomatic and substance-use samples.

A 2025 meta-analysis of 40 eating-disorder and anxiety-disorder studies also found a moderate overall discrepancy, g = .41, 95% CI [.28, .53], with clients typically reporting stronger alliances than therapists.
text.formatted: A 2025 meta-analysis of 40 eating-disorder and anxiety-disorder studies also found a moderate overall discrepancy, g = .41, 95% CI <ref type="bibr">[.28, .53]</ref>, with clients typically reporting stronger alliances than therapists.

text.text: The discrepancy was not moderated by diagnostic group, treatment orientation, or assessment timing (Lev Ari et al., 2025).
text.formatted: The discrepancy was not moderated by diagnostic group, treatment orientation, or assessment timing <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Lev Ari et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, a therapist's lower rating should not automatically be interpreted as a lack of skill or pessimism.

Across several studies, moderately lower therapist ratings were associated with equal or better outcomes, possibly because a cautious therapist remains attentive to unspoken clinical concerns (e.g., Chen et al., 2022; Kivlighan & Marmarosh, 2018; Li et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Across several studies, moderately lower therapist ratings were associated with equal or better outcomes, possibly because a cautious therapist remains attentive to unspoken clinical concerns (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Chen et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Kivlighan & Marmarosh, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Li et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Research on trainee therapists supports this general pattern.

For example, Bar-Kalifa et al. (2016) showed that trainee therapists were able to track clients' session-to-session fluctuations in their functioning, without significant average over-or underestimation.
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Bar-Kalifa et al. (2016)</ref> showed that trainee therapists were able to track clients' session-to-session fluctuations in their functioning, without significant average over-or underestimation.

text.text: Yet, trainee therapists' underestimation can sometimes reflect specific personal difficulties (Kivlighan & Marmarosh, 2018).
text.formatted: Yet, trainee therapists' underestimation can sometimes reflect specific personal difficulties <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Kivlighan & Marmarosh, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: In one study, graduate student counselors rated the alliance lower than clients, and counselor attachment anxiety was associated with a larger negative discrepancy.

Thus, modest therapist caution may be adaptive, but persistent underestimation accompanied by poor tracking of the client's actual experience may reflect trainee anxiety rather than enhanced clinical vigilance (Kivlighan & Marmarosh, 2018).
text.formatted: Thus, modest therapist caution may be adaptive, but persistent underestimation accompanied by poor tracking of the client's actual experience may reflect trainee anxiety rather than enhanced clinical vigilance <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Kivlighan & Marmarosh, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Past literature emphasizes the clinical significance of examining perceptions from both therapists and clients.
Some highlight the importance of examining the level at which their agreement occurs, the direction of disagreement, and sometimes the point in treatment at which ratings are obtained.

For example, Zilcha-Mano et al. (2017) found that client-therapist alliance congruence predicted their symptom levels approximately one month later; congruence explained a significant additional variance beyond therapist-reported alliance.
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr">Zilcha-Mano et al. (2017)</ref> found that client-therapist alliance congruence predicted their symptom levels approximately one month later; congruence explained a significant additional variance beyond therapist-reported alliance.

text.text: However, evidence also suggests that jointly high ratings are more associated with improvement than agreement alone.

For example, Marmarosh and Kivlighan (2012) found that, among therapist-client dyads, sessions were perceived as smoother when the client and the therapist agreed that the alliance was strong, compared to agreement at a low alliance level.
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Marmarosh and Kivlighan (2012)</ref> found that, among therapist-client dyads, sessions were perceived as smoother when the client and the therapist agreed that the alliance was strong, compared to agreement at a low alliance level.

text.text: Clients perceived sessions as less smooth when they rated the alliance lower than their therapists did.
Further, positive therapist-client agreement early in treatment predicted greater symptom improvement.
Similarly, Dietel et al. (2026) found that client and therapist ratings were moderately correlated, and clients again rated the alliance more positively.
text.formatted: Similarly, <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Dietel et al. (2026)</ref> found that client and therapist ratings were moderately correlated, and clients again rated the alliance more positively.

text.text: Jointly high ratings predicted greater reductions in depression and general distress, but congruence by itself did not predict outcomes, and there were no significant directional effects of incongruence.
These findings caution against treating therapist-client perceptual agreement as intrinsically therapeutic.
High therapist-high client agreement may be favorable primarily because both participants experience a strong alliance, not necessarily because their scores are identical (Dietel et al., 2026).
text.formatted: High therapist-high client agreement may be favorable primarily because both participants experience a strong alliance, not necessarily because their scores are identical <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Dietel et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Studies recognize the importance of examining session-to-session perceptions, as therapist-client perception alignment is partly state-like.
For example, Chen et al. (2018) showed that time in treatment was associated with greater temporal therapist-client congruence and lower directional discrepancy.
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Chen et al. (2018)</ref> showed that time in treatment was associated with greater temporal therapist-client congruence and lower directional discrepancy.

text.text: Synchrony was stronger for the bond dimension of alliance than for agreement about tasks and goals, suggesting that therapists may find changes in relational warmth easier to detect than changes in treatment rationale or therapeutic activities (Chen et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Synchrony was stronger for the bond dimension of alliance than for agreement about tasks and goals, suggesting that therapists may find changes in relational warmth easier to detect than changes in treatment rationale or therapeutic activities <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Chen et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Research also shows that the implications of agreement can vary by treatment phase. Laws et al. (2017) revealed that over 12 sessions of psychotherapy for depression, clients' and therapists' alliance ratings became more convergent.
text.formatted: Research also shows that the implications of agreement can vary by treatment phase. <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Laws et al. (2017)</ref> revealed that over 12 sessions of psychotherapy for depression, clients' and therapists' alliance ratings became more convergent.

text.text: Alliance convergence was associated with greater reductions in self-rated depression three months later.

In an 11-session cognitive behavioral treatment, Moshe-Cohen et al. (2024) found that early in therapy, the combined strength of client and therapist alliance ratings predicted lower posttreatment symptoms and a lower probability of dropout, regardless of the exact level of agreement.

(2024)</ref> found that early in therapy, the combined strength of client and therapist alliance ratings predicted lower posttreatment symptoms and a lower probability of dropout, regardless of the exact level of agreement.

text.text: Late in treatment, however, outcomes were worse when therapists rated the alliance more positively than clients did, which may signal that the therapist failed to recognize ongoing dissatisfaction or inadequate therapeutic progress.

Furthermore, studies have linked the agreement levels to clients' symptoms and functioning. Atzil-Slonim et al. (2015) found that therapist and client ratings showed substantial temporal correspondence, although therapists generally gave lower ratings.

(2015)</ref> found that therapist and client ratings showed substantial temporal correspondence, although therapists generally gave lower ratings.

text.text: Overall, session-level studies and literature on trainee therapists alike suggest that therapist recognition of the client's experience is associated with clients' current distress, nextsession symptom change, and longer-term treatment outcomes.
However, the literature is not yet large or uniform enough to conclude that shared perspectives between therapists and clients always predict improvement.

The available research, therefore, supports routine dyadic monitoring and session-level analysis while also indicating the need for additional longitudinal studies that distinguish alliance strength, directional discrepancy, current versus future symptoms, and dimensions of alliance.

In addition, current variable-centered approaches that separately track accuracy or directional bias may overlook the interdependent nature of dyadic interactions, in which multiple perceptual processes operate simultaneously (i.e., the "dyadic dance" between therapists and clients).

To resolve this, Li (2022) identified two latent groups of therapist-client dyads: dyadic independence, in which therapists and clients demonstrate self-consistency but non-significant influence on one another's scores, and mutual influence, in which their perceptions influence each other.

However, no known study has examined latent configurations of sessions, which may help classify sessions based on distinct combinations of therapist-client synchrony, revealing clinically intuitive and commonly occurring patterns that remain obscured when relational parameters are analyzed separately (Vermunt, 2003).

text.text: Linking these patterns to client outcomes, both concurrently and prospectively, will generate clinically informed decisions for treatment planning, ongoing monitoring, and revisions to the alliance process, as well as feedback for use in supervision with a therapist-in-training.

The present study extends prior research by identifying distinct session-level patterns of therapists' and clients' perceptions of the therapeutic alliance and treatment progress and by examining whether these patterns are associated with client-reported treatment outcomes, among a sample of therapists in training.
We focused on two client outcomes: personal functioning and psychological symptoms.
Personal functioning reflects clients' ability to manage their daily roles and relationships effectively, whereas psychological symptoms indicate their current level of emotional distress.
Both domains are commonly assessed in studies of treatment effectiveness, particularly in naturalistic clinical settings (e.g., Chen et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Both domains are commonly assessed in studies of treatment effectiveness, particularly in naturalistic clinical settings (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Chen et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Using longitudinal data from both clients and therapists, we adopted a latent class analytic approach to classify sessions according to therapist and client ratings.

We then used multilevel models to examine whether these session-level patterns were associated with clients' current and subsequent functioning and psychological symptoms, controlling for clients' scores at the preceding session.

Accounting for prior-session outcomes reduces the influence of temporal stability and provides a more stringent test of whether therapist-client session configurations were associated with changes in client well-being over time.
This approach extends prior research, as not all studies of alliance agreement have accounted for clients' outcomes at the preceding session.
We addressed two research questions.
First, would there be distinct session-level patterns of therapist and client ratings?
Second, which patterns predict better concurrent and subsequent client outcomes, as indicated by fewer psychological symptoms and higher personal functioning?
Based on prior evidence, we expected to identify multiple patterns of therapist and client ratings.

We further hypothesized that sessions characterized by shared favorable perceptions would be associated with fewer psychological symptoms and better personal functioning both concurrently and at the subsequent session.
Data for the present study were collected at one on-campus couple and family therapy training center in the southeastern United States.

Participants followed the study protocol of a larger Practice Research Network (PRN) consortium that uses shared assessment and datacollection procedures to improve the quality of practice-based research in marriage and family therapy (MFT; Johnson et al., 2017).

text.text: Eligible clients were individuals who sought treatment at the center and consented to participate in the PRN project.
The analytic sample included 86 adult clients who received individual therapy across a total of 1,035 sessions.
Clients attended an average of 12.03 sessions (SD = 12.73, range = 1-56).
Of the clients, 28 identified as male and 58 identified as female.
Their mean age was 24.95 years (SD = 9.29, range = 18-85).
Most clients identified as White (64.9%), followed by Black or African American (17.5%), Hispanic (10.5%), Asian (5.3%), or another racial or ethnic group (1.8%).

Regarding relationship status, 7.0% of clients were married, 17.4% were in a relationship and cohabiting, 25.6% were in a committed relationship but were not cohabiting, and 50.0% were single, separated, or divorced.
Most clients reported an annual household income below $20,000 (72.1%); 23.3% reported an income between $20,000 and $50,000, and 4.6% reported an income above $50,000.

Clients' highest levels of education included a GED or high school diploma (29.1%), vocational or technical school education (3.5%), an associate degree or approximately 2 years of college education (31.4%), a bachelor's degree (24.4%), or a graduate or professional degree (11.6%).
Fifteen therapists in the study were enrolled in a doctoral program accredited by the Commission on Accreditation for Marriage and Family Therapy Education (COAMFTE).
Each therapist had completed a master's degree in MFT or a related mental health discipline and had accumulated at least 300 hours of direct client contact.

text.text: The questionnaire assessed therapists' perceptions of the therapeutic alliance, withinsession progress, and overall progress toward treatment goals.
Alliance was assessed with the item "Therapy alliance within this session," rated from 0 (very poor) to 6 (excellent).
Withinsession progress was assessed with the item "Client(s) progress within this session," rated from 0 (major digress) to 4 (major progress).

text.text: The measure assesses three dimensions of the alliance: bond, agreement on therapeutic goals, and agreement on therapeutic tasks.
Its 13 items are rated on a 7-point Likert-type scale ranging from 1 (completely disagree) to 7 (strongly agree).

Sample items included "I do not feel accepted by the therapist" (bond), "The therapist and I are not in agreement about the goals for this therapy" (goals), and "The therapist does not understand me" (tasks).
Negatively worded items were reverse-coded so that higher scores reflected a stronger therapeutic alliance.
In the current study, the Cronbach's alpha was .79 for bond, .86 for goals, and .60 for tasks.
Clients rated their personal functioning after each session using the functioning subscale of the Intersession Report questionnaire (Johnson et al., 2010).

Item scores were combined to create a total functioning score, with higher scores indicating better personal functioning.

Items were rated on a 7-point scale ranging from 1 (almost never) to 7 (almost all the time).
Scores were combined to form a total symptom score, with higher scores indicating greater psychological distress.
The measure demonstrated acceptable internal consistency in the current study (Cronbach's α = .77).

text.text: MLCA was chosen because the data had a hierarchical structure, with repeated session assessments nested within clients.
Preliminary analysis tested an unconditional three-level model to examine therapist-level effects where sessions were nested within clients who were then nested within therapists.

The intra-class correlation (ICC) on the therapist-level was .075-.084 for client-rated therapeutic alliance variables, .046-.063 for therapist-rated session variables, and .023-.041 for client-rated outcome variables.
As the differences among therapists were small in magnitude (ICCs < .10) and we had a relatively small sample, we decided to estimate only two-level models (sessions nested within clients).

text.text: A series of two-level multilevel models specifying two through six within-client latent classes was estimated using six indicators: therapist-rated alliance, within-session progress, and overall progress toward treatment goals, as well as client-rated bond, goals, and tasks.

The optimal number of classes was selected using several criteria: (a) the Bayesian information criterion (BIC), with lower values indicating better relative fit; (b) the bootstrapped likelihood ratio test (BLRT), which compared a model containing k classes with a model containing k -1 classes; (c) adequate class size, defined as at least 1% of the observed sessions; and (d) the conceptual interpretability and distinctiveness of the resulting classes (Jung & Wickrama, 2008).

The present study identified distinct session-level patterns of therapists' and clients' perceptions of the therapeutic alliance and progress, and examined whether these patterns are associated with client-reported treatment outcomes.
Findings of this study have significant implications for treatment planning, ongoing monitoring, adaptation to the treatment process, and supervision of therapists-in-training.

The identification of five session types-all high, bond focused, goals/tasks focused, client low, and all low-demonstrates that therapist-client perceptions cannot be adequately represented by a single total score or a simple therapist-client difference score.
Instead, sessionlevel therapist-client perceptions appear to form qualitatively distinct configurations and components.

This person-centered finding extends prior therapist-client dyad research, which has generally examined linear agreement, directional discrepancy, or temporal congruence (Igra et al., 2020; Lev Ari et al., 2025).

This predominance is consistent with previous research showing that alliance ratings tend to be concentrated toward the positive end of their response scales (Tryon et al., 2007 (Tryon et al., , 2008)).

text.text: Thus, the frequency of the all-high pattern may partly reflect the generally positive alliances developed in the present clinical setting, as lower-score clients tended to prematurely leave therapy (Tryon et al., 2007 (Tryon et al., , 2008)).
text.formatted: Thus, the frequency of the all-high pattern may partly reflect the generally positive alliances developed in the present clinical setting, as lower-score clients tended to prematurely leave therapy <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Tryon et al., 2007</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Tryon et al., , 2008))</ref>.

text.text: Nevertheless, nearly half of the sessions were classified into one of the four alternative patterns, indicating meaningful session-to-session heterogeneity.
The most consistent outcome differences involved the client-low sessions, accounting for nearly 20% of the sessions.
Following these sessions, clients reported poorer current personal functioning and more current psychological symptoms than after all-high or bond-focused sessions.

Yet, the concurrent findings may not establish causal associations, as alliance and symptoms are known to demonstrate reciprocal within-person associations (Atzil-Slonim et al., 2015; Flückiger, Rubel, et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Yet, the concurrent findings may not establish causal associations, as alliance and symptoms are known to demonstrate reciprocal within-person associations <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Atzil-Slonim et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Flückiger, Rubel, et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: The next-session findings provide stronger evidence of temporal ordering.
Client-low sessions predicted higher symptoms at the following session than did all-high or bond-focused sessions, controlling for previous symptoms.

This result is consistent with prospective session-level evidence, such as Rubel et al. (2018), who found that higher therapist-client bond ratings predicted fewer next-session symptoms when the ratings were congruent, and Li et al. (2024), who found that session-specific therapist accuracy and discrepancy predicted symptom change before the next session.
text.formatted: This result is consistent with prospective session-level evidence, such as <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Rubel et al. (2018)</ref>, who found that higher therapist-client bond ratings predicted fewer next-session symptoms when the ratings were congruent, and <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Li et al. (2024)</ref>, who found that session-specific therapist accuracy and discrepancy predicted symptom change before the next session.

text.text: These results are also consistent with other between-dyad evidence that disagreement may be most concerning when therapists view the alliance more positively than clients (Marmarosh & Kivlighan, 2012; Moshe-Cohen et al., 2024).
text.formatted: These results are also consistent with other between-dyad evidence that disagreement may be most concerning when therapists view the alliance more positively than clients <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Marmarosh & Kivlighan, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Moshe-Cohen et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Together with the present findings, this suggests that a client-low session may reflect an underrecognized clinical difficulty.

When therapists continue to perceive the treatment process positively despite low client scores, they may be less likely to invite corrective feedback, reconsider the treatment focus, or address an emerging rupture.
The discrepancy may therefore persist beyond the immediate session and interfere with the client's symptom reduction (Rubel et al., 2018).
text.formatted: The discrepancy may therefore persist beyond the immediate session and interfere with the client's symptom reduction <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Rubel et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Notably, we did not identify a therapist-low pattern, despite evidence suggesting therapist underestimation of alliance in both general (e.g., Chen et al., 2022; Flückiger et al., 2018; Rubel et al., 2018) and trainee samples (e.g., Kivlighan & Marmarosh, 2018; Li et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Notably, we did not identify a therapist-low pattern, despite evidence suggesting therapist underestimation of alliance in both general (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Chen et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Flückiger et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Rubel et al., 2018)</ref> and trainee samples (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Kivlighan & Marmarosh, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Li et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: This may be due to our different assessments used with therapists and clients and the limited variability of the therapist-reported alliance score.

This may also be caused by our MLCA approach, whereas the latent classes recognize session-level patterns, the multiple-level analyses also highlighted within-individual variations beyond between-individual differences.
In comparison, past literature may have only compared therapist-client pairs or did not distinguish between versus within-individual differences.
This finding, thus, will need to be replicated in larger longitudinal samples with analyses on session-level patterns.

The bond-focused sessions accounted for 16.3% of all sessions and were associated with outcomes comparable to those of all-high sessions, and better current personal functioning and lower next-session symptoms than client-low sessions.
This finding may suggest that a strong affective connection can provide an important relational foundation, even when agreement on treatment goals or tasks is comparatively less pronounced.

However, the finding alone should not be interpreted as evidence that goal and task alliance are unimportant. Bordin's model (1979) conceptualizes bond, goals, and tasks as interdependent components of the working alliance, and meta-analytic evidence indicates that goal consensus and task collaboration contribute to treatment outcome, and sometimes more strongly than the bond component (Tryon et al., 2018; Webb et al., 2011).
text.formatted: However, the finding alone should not be interpreted as evidence that goal and task alliance are unimportant. <ref type="bibr">Bordin's model (1979)</ref> conceptualizes bond, goals, and tasks as interdependent components of the working alliance, and meta-analytic evidence indicates that goal consensus and task collaboration contribute to treatment outcome, and sometimes more strongly than the bond component <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Tryon et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Webb et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: The present results may thus suggest that a strong bond can coexist with favorable short-term outcomes, but they may not demonstrate that the bond can compensate for unresolved disagreements over goals and tasks in therapeutic work.
We did not detect a difference in concurrent or subsequent outcomes between all-low or goals/tasks-focused sessions and other sessions.
These null findings require cautious interpretation.
The goals/tasks-focused class represented only 3.3% of sessions, and the all-low class accounted for 8.5%.

Estimates based on these comparatively rare classes are likely to suggest smaller statistical power and should not be interpreted as evidence that these patterns are equivalent to the more prevalent profiles.
The goals/tasks-focused pattern may represent a more instrumental form of therapeutic collaboration.
The therapist and the client may agree about the problems to address, the procedures to use, and the progress made in resolving the problems, even though the affective bond can be less developed.
Such a configuration could be sufficient for productive work in structured, problem-focused, or skills-based sessions.
The rarity of the profile may nevertheless indicate that a strong goal-and-task collaboration usually develops alongside at least a moderately positive bond.
Some evidence suggests that when training therapists recognized the goals and tasks of clients, clients rated the sessions more favorably (Fitzpatrick et al., 2005).
text.formatted: Some evidence suggests that when training therapists recognized the goals and tasks of clients, clients rated the sessions more favorably <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Fitzpatrick et al., 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Still, further research is needed to determine the implications of goals/tasks-focused sessions.

The null finding for all-low sessions may initially appear inconsistent with studies showing that high therapist-high client agreement is more favorable than low therapist-low client agreement (e.g., Dietel et al., 2026; Marmarosh & Kivlighan, 2012).
text.formatted: The null finding for all-low sessions may initially appear inconsistent with studies showing that high therapist-high client agreement is more favorable than low therapist-low client agreement (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Dietel et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Marmarosh & Kivlighan, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: One possibility is that an all-low session represents a recognized clinical difficulty acknowledged by both participants.
Their shared recognition may increase the likelihood that the problem will be discussed or that the therapist will adjust treatment.
By contrast, in a client-low session, the therapist may be unaware that the client is disengaged or dissatisfied.

Alliance-rupture research indicates that ruptures are not uniformly detrimental; rupture-repair episodes can contribute to favorable outcomes when therapists and clients use them to renegotiate their relationship and therapeutic work (Eubanks et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Alliance-rupture research indicates that ruptures are not uniformly detrimental; rupture-repair episodes can contribute to favorable outcomes when therapists and clients use them to renegotiate their relationship and therapeutic work <ref type="bibr">(Eubanks et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: It is also possible that some all-low sessions involved difficult but therapeutically productive work.

Challenging established interpersonal patterns, discussing painful material, or negotiating disagreement may temporarily lower both participants' session evaluations without producing immediate deterioration.

Notably, the latent classes were based on relative rather than absolute levels, and the "low" ratings may not necessarily represent clinically poor alliances (as the multilevel analyses accounted for mean scores at the individual level).
Taken together, the results suggest that neither agreement alone nor alliance level alone fully explains the clinical significance of therapist-client perception patterns.
All-high sessions were generally favorable, but bond-focused sessions produced similarly favorable outcomes despite relatively weaker goal or task ratings.
Conversely, all-low agreement was not significantly associated with worse outcomes, whereas the discrepant client-low pattern was consistently associated with poorer functioning and higher symptoms.
This multi-informant, longitudinal study contributes to the literature by demonstrating that session-level therapist-client ratings form distinct and clinically meaningful configurations.

The prospective association between client-low sessions and next-session symptoms provides particularly important evidence that an underrecognized clinical difficulty may have consequences extending beyond the immediate session.
However, this study is not without limitations.

First, several factors limit the generalizability of the findings, including the geographic location, the trainee context, and the relatively lower-resourced client sample, and potential social desirability in rating sessions.
Clients may hesitate to provide critical feedback when completing ratings in the treatment setting, particularly if they expect their therapist to see their responses.
Regular supervision may also have increased attention to how trainees evaluate their work and to opportunities to respond to client concerns, which may differ from a naturalistic therapy setting.

We also acknowledge that Hispanic ethnicity and racial identities are not mutually exclusive; however, the present dataset included Hispanic as a response option in the race variable, which did not allow Hispanic participants to report their racial identity separately.
Second, due to a lack of data, the therapist and client ratings were not measured using the same assessment tool.
As such, their scores (especially client-low) should be interpreted as relative to other sessions rather than relative to each informant.

Third, we only predicted client functioning and symptom levels at the next session, although some evidence suggests that the effects may emerge longer-term, such as several sessions later (Zilcha-Mano et al., 2015; 2017), which should be addressed in future studies.
text.formatted: Third, we only predicted client functioning and symptom levels at the next session, although some evidence suggests that the effects may emerge longer-term, such as several sessions later <ref type="bibr">(Zilcha-Mano et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr">2017)</ref>, which should be addressed in future studies.

text.text: Additionally, although a strength of the study was its identification of session-level configurations beyond the vast evidence on therapist-client pairs, the analyses accounted for sessions nested within clients but not for clients nested within therapists.

Shared therapist influences, including systematic differences in rating tendencies and treatment delivery, may have affected both the identified session profiles and their associations with client outcomes.
Moreover, missing data also limit the interpretation of the findings, particularly because therapist ratings were unavailable for a proportion of sessions.
Missingness was associated with some observed client and session characteristics, and potential dependence on unobserved factors cannot be ruled out.
Thus, model-based handling of missing data may not fully eliminate bias.
Moreover, subsequent outcome models treated most-likely class assignments as observed and did not incorporate classification uncertainty.
These limitations warrant caution when interpreting the profiles and their associations with client outcomes.

Finally, the measure of psychological symptoms only captured internalizing symptoms; however, clients also may experience externalizing symptoms or other concerns that were not captured by the current measures.

Future research is recommended to replicate the configurations across clinics and levels of therapist experience, use parallel measures when the aim is to study therapist-client agreement, and examine whether therapist progress ratings add information beyond client alliance and prior symptoms.
Studies should also address therapist clustering, missing reporter data, social desirability, and classification uncertainty to provide more robust evidence.
Clinically, the findings support the importance of routinely collecting client ratings rather than relying solely on therapist judgment.
Nearly one in five sessions was classified as client-low in our trainee sample, indicating that potentially meaningful therapist-client discrepancies were not rare.

For therapists, reviewing session-specific ratings could help identify occasions when clients feel less connected, less confident in treatment goals, or less engaged with therapeutic tasks than therapists realize.

The ratings can open a conversation with clients as an opportunity to reassess and improve treatment, and clinicians can ask separately about feeling understood, the relevance of treatment goals, and the usefulness of session activities.
In supervision, trainees can examine client feedback alongside their own evaluations and distinguish feeling that a session went well from evidence that the client experienced it that way.
Supervisors can help trainees consider specific moments in the session, practice inviting critical feedback, and identify an adjustment to discuss collaboratively with the client.
Discrepancies in perceptions should be treated as information rather than evidence that either participant is "wrong."
By facilitating more coordinated "dance" between therapists and clients, better treatment outcomes can be achieved.
